aave.name: Aave
aave.AssetStrategy:
Asset strategy. Aave v3 on Ethereum runs the widest curated asset list of the five protocols, 67 reserves in the Core market alone as returned by the [Aave v3 GraphQL API](https://aave.com/docs/aave-v3/getting-started/graphql.md), and it manages that breadth with tiering rather than exclusion: blue chip collateral (WETH, wstETH, WBTC, cbBTC) keeps a full loan to value, while a large second tier of yield bearing and synthetic dollar assets (USDe, sUSDe, rsETH, osETH, DAI, LINK, XAUt) is set to LTV 0 so it can only be used inside E-Mode or as pure supply, with a liquidation threshold still active to protect legacy positions. Almost every non trivial reserve carries an explicit supply cap and borrow cap, and dozens of borrow caps are set to the sentinel value 1, which switches an asset to collateral only in practice. Pricing is standardised on Chainlink feeds wrapped in Aave's own capped adapters (CAPO), described in the [Aave oracle documentation](https://aave.com/docs/ecosystem/oracle.md) as the two oracle types in production. The strategic distinguishing feature is the risk steward and guardian layer: after the April 2026 rsETH bridge exploit the Guardian froze rsETH, wrsETH and even WETH across deployments within hours, per the [Aave rsETH incident report](https://governance.aave.com/t/rseth-incident-report-april-20-2026/24580), which is why several large reserves in the table below sit frozen or at LTV 0 today.

Market: Aave v3 Ethereum Core, Pool `0x87870Bca3F3fD6335C3F4ce8392D69350B4fA4E2`. Parameters read from [the Pool contract](https://etherscan.io/address/0x87870Bca3F3fD6335C3F4ce8392D69350B4fA4E2#readProxyContract); price sources from [AaveOracle](https://etherscan.io/address/0x54586bE62E3c3580375aE3723C145253060Ca0C2#readContract). TypedRisks.name: Unbacked LRT collateral minted through a partner bridge
TypedRisks.description: An attacker extracted 152,577 rsETH from the Kelp LayerZero lockbox and supplied unbacked rsETH into Aave as collateral. The Guardian froze rsETH and wrsETH from 18:52 UTC on 18 April 2026 across eleven deployments.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Guardian freeze of rsETH and wrsETH, V4 Protocol Security Council disabling supply and borrow at the Core Hub and Kelp E Spoke
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Supply of a collateral asset growing faster than the issuer's verifiable backing, plus any single-address deposit that moves a market cap in one block

TypedRisks.name: Residual bad debt gap after recoveries
TypedRisks.description: The original shortfall was about 163,183 ETH and recoveries brought it down to roughly 120,015 ETH, leaving a residual gap of about 75,081 ETH. Closing the gap depends on voluntary contributions rather than protocol reserves.
TypedRisks.mitigation: DeFi United coalition contributions of 14,570 ETH, a Mantle credit facility of up to 30,000 ETH, and a requested 25,000 ETH DAO treasury donation
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Residual ETH shortfall versus committed and funded recovery pledges, tracked weekly

TypedRisks.name: Treasury concentration in the native token
TypedRisks.description: Buybacks were paused from 19 April 2026 to preserve balance sheet flexibility, and forum commentary notes that over 50 percent of the treasury is held in AAVE. A treasury dominated by its own governance token loses value exactly when it is needed to absorb a deficit.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Buyback pause to retain stablecoin flexibility during the recovery period
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Share of treasury held in AAVE versus stablecoins, and AAVE price drawdown during a deficit event

TypedRisks.name: Illiquid governance-token collateral used for a short squeeze
TypedRisks.description: In November 2022 an actor borrowed about 47 million USD of CRV against USDC on Aave V2 Ethereum in an attempted squeeze, leaving roughly 1.6 million USD of bad debt. Thin on-chain liquidity meant liquidations could not clear the position at book value.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Legacy V2 markets wound down, borrow caps and isolation mode on long-tail assets in V3
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Ratio of a single borrower's position size to on-chain DEX depth for the collateral asset
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: Aave DAO incident and bad debt thread

TypedRisks.name: Stranded bad debt on non-Ethereum deployments from bridge failures
TypedRisks.description: The Multichain bridge collapse in July 2023 and the Harmony bridge hack in June 2022 left scattered pockets of unrecoverable bad debt on non-Ethereum V2 and V3 deployments. These positions cannot be liquidated because the underlying bridged assets are permanently impaired.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Recognition and quantification of the legacy pockets in the DAO bad debt accounting exercise
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Bridged asset price divergence from the canonical asset, and non-liquidatable position count per deployment
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: Aave DAO incident and bad debt thread

TypedRisks.name: Automatic slashing of staked aTokens under Umbrella
TypedRisks.description: Umbrella is the automated Safety Module: users stake aTokens and are slashed automatically when a deficit is recorded, isolated per asset and network pair. Stakers therefore bear first loss on the specific reserve they backstop.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Isolation per asset and network pair, plus DAO deficit offsets such as the first 100,000 USDT absorbed by the DAO
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Recorded deficit per Umbrella reserve versus the staked backstop balance for that reserve

TypedRisks.name: Backstop capacity too small for a tail deficit
TypedRisks.description: Umbrella was sized against historical deficits of roughly 0.000004 percent of outstanding borrows per month, a scale far below the rsETH shortfall. A single collateral-issuer failure can produce a deficit orders of magnitude larger than the modelled base rate.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Deficit offsets, staged loss waterfall from stakers to depositors to the DAO treasury
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Ratio of Umbrella staked value to the largest single-asset exposure in each reserve

TypedRisks.name: Novel V4 Hub and Spoke architecture
TypedRisks.description: Aave V4 activated on Ethereum mainnet with Core, Prime and Plus hubs and asset-specific spokes, a materially different design from V3. New code paths mean new unknown failure modes despite extensive review.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Around 345 days of cumulative security review, a 1.5 million USD security budget, audits by Trail of Bits, Blackthorn and ChainSecurity, and flash loans initially disabled
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Unexpected reverts or accounting drift in hub and spoke reconciliation, and any deviation between hub-level and spoke-level accounting
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: ARFC Aave V4 activation on Ethereum mainnet

TypedRisks.name: Cross-hub credit line contagion
TypedRisks.description: V4 supports cross-hub credit lines, letting liquidity and therefore losses propagate between Core, Prime and Plus. A deficit that starts in one spoke can be transmitted to hubs that never listed the impaired asset.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Add caps and draw caps per spoke, plus Protocol Security Council emergency powers during the hardening period
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Drawn amount on each cross-hub credit line versus its draw cap, and change in cross-hub exposure per epoch
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: ARFC Aave V4 activation on Ethereum mainnet

TypedRisks.name: Oracle design for yield-bearing and fixed-maturity collateral
TypedRisks.description: V4 prices assets with Chainlink SVR variants, CAPO adapters for yield-bearing and stable assets, Pendle linear discount adapters for principal tokens, and prices USDe at the USDT secondary market price. Each adapter is a modelling assumption rather than a direct market quote.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Chainlink SVR feeds, CAPO growth caps, and per-adapter parameterisation reviewed during the V4 security process
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Adapter output divergence from the DEX mid price beyond a set tolerance, and oracle staleness above the configured heartbeat
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: ARFC Aave V4 activation on Ethereum mainnet

TypedRisks.name: Concentrated emergency powers in a small council
TypedRisks.description: The Protocol Security Council holds emergency powers during the V4 hardening period and used them to disable supply and borrow at the Core Hub and Kelp E Spoke. The same powers that stopped the rsETH bleed could be misused or fail to act.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Documented scope of council powers, time-limited hardening period, public disclosure of each emergency action
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Number and scope of emergency actions taken without a prior on-chain vote

TypedRisks.name: Guardian freezes trapping unrelated depositors
TypedRisks.description: The Protocol Guardian froze WETH alongside rsETH on Core, Prime, Arbitrum, Base, Mantle and Linea. Freezing a base asset protects solvency but blocks withdrawal and liquidation for users with no exposure to the impaired collateral.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Freezes scoped per asset and per deployment rather than protocol-wide, with public incident threads
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Duration of any asset freeze, and the number of deployments frozen simultaneously

TypedRisks.name: Deposit flight and utilisation spike after a solvency scare
TypedRisks.description: Aave TVL fell from 26.4 billion USD to roughly 18 billion USD after the Kelp exploit, against a wider 13 billion USD DeFi outflow in 48 hours. High utilisation blocks withdrawals and prevents liquidators from clearing positions.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Interest rate curves that spike above the kink, plus asset freezes that stop further borrowing
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Reserve utilisation above the kink for more than 48 hours, and net deposit outflow per 24 hours
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: Streetbrief coverage of the Kelp exploit and Aave liquidity crisis

TypedRisks.name: Concentrated synthetic dollar exposure in dedicated spokes
TypedRisks.description: V4 launched Ethena Ecosystem and Correlated Spokes carrying PT-sUSDe, PT-USDe, sUSDe and USDe. The design concentrates a single issuer's credit and funding risk into named spokes.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Spoke isolation with add caps and draw caps, USDe priced at the USDT secondary market price rather than hardcoded at one dollar
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: sUSDe redemption backlog, Ethena funding rate sign and magnitude, and spoke utilisation against caps
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: ARFC Aave V4 activation on Ethereum mainnet

TypedRisks.name: Sanctioned-actor nexus in a major loss event
TypedRisks.description: The Kelp exploit was attributed to Lazarus and TraderTraitor, which places state-linked actors at the centre of an Aave loss event. Recovery coordination and any negotiated return of funds carry sanctions and reporting exposure.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Coordination with issuers and chain security councils rather than direct negotiation, public on-chain tracing of the attacker addresses
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Attribution updates from incident responders, and any address in the recovery flow appearing on a sanctions list
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: Streetbrief coverage of the Kelp exploit and Aave liquidity crisis

aave.RiskPosture: Aave's risk profile has shifted decisively from smart contract risk toward collateral issuer and counterparty risk. The core lending logic has held up, but the protocol's willingness to list high-LTV liquid restaking collateral means that a failure anywhere in a partner's minting or bridging stack becomes an Aave solvency event, which is exactly what happened with Kelp and LayerZero in April 2026 ([LlamaRisk](https://governance.aave.com/t/rseth-incident-2026-04-18/24481)). The protocol's crisis machinery works: Guardian freezes were executed within hours and roughly 54 percent of the shortfall was recovered ([TokenLogic](https://governance.aave.com/t/arfc-rseth-incident-funding-update/24740)). What is weak is loss absorption. Umbrella was calibrated against historical deficits measured in millionths of a percent of borrows ([Aave docs](https://aave.com/help/umbrella/umbrella)), the treasury is over half AAVE and buybacks are paused ([Aave governance](https://governance.aave.com/t/arfc-pause-aave-buybacks/24686)), and the residual gap is being closed by a voluntary coalition rather than by protocol capital. Layered on top is a freshly activated V4 hub and spoke architecture with cross-hub credit lines and model-based oracle adapters ([Aave governance](https://governance.aave.com/t/arfc-aave-v4-activation-on-ethereum-mainnet/24293)), which raises technological risk during the hardening period. Net posture: high severity, issuer-driven, with mitigation depending on discretionary emergency powers and external goodwill.

compound.name: Compound
compound.AssetStrategy:
Asset strategy. Compound III (Comet) does not run a shared pool. Each market has one borrowable base asset and a short list of collateral that can only be used to borrow that base, which structurally isolates every asset pair, as set out in the [Compound III documentation](https://docs.compound.finance/). On Ethereum there are six live markets: USDC, USDT, WETH, WBTC, wstETH and USDS. Collateral is capped in native units, and Compound uses a two factor system, a `borrowCollateralFactor` for opening capacity and a higher `liquidateCollateralFactor` for solvency, with a separate `liquidationFactor` penalty; the liquidator's discount is `StoreFrontPriceFactor * (1e18 - liquidationFactor)` per [the liquidation docs](https://docs.compound.finance/liquidation/). The distinguishing feature is how aggressively Compound deprecates: assets it wants to remove are left listed with a supply cap of 0 and a liquidate factor of 0.0001, which is exactly how deUSD and sdeUSD read today after the Elixir collapse. In the tables the "Liq. bonus" column is the implied penalty, 1 minus liquidationFactor.

Parameters read from each Comet proxy. Bases: USDC `0xc3d688B66703497DAA19211EEdff47f25384cdc3`, USDT `0x3Afdc9BCA9213A35503b077a6072F3D0d5AB0840`, WETH `0xA17581A9E3356d9A858b789D68B4d866e593aE94`, WBTC `0xe85Dc543813B8c2CFEaAc371517b925a166a9293`, wstETH `0x3D0bb1ccaB520A66e607822fC55BC921738fAFE3`, USDS `0x5D409e56D886231aDAf00c8775665AD0f9897b56`.

TypedRisks.name: Governance proposal code defects reaching production
TypedRisks.description: Proposal 62 shipped a comparison operator bug, greater-than instead of greater-than-or-equal, in two locations of the reward distribution logic. Roughly 280,000 COMP worth about 82.88 million USD became claimable in error.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Post-incident emphasis on audit of proposal payloads before execution
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Diff coverage and independent review sign-off on every executable proposal payload before the voting period closes
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: CryptoSlate on the Compound distribution bug

TypedRisks.name: Oracle upgrade breaking a live market
TypedRisks.description: Proposal 117 upgraded the price oracle to a version that assumed every cToken exposes an underlying() function, which cETH does not, so getUnderlyingPrice reverted. The cETH market was frozen for supply, borrow, withdraw and liquidation for eight days.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Proposal 119 restored a working feed, and OpenZeppelin published a public post-mortem
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Simulated getUnderlyingPrice call across every listed cToken as a mandatory pre-execution check

TypedRisks.name: Oracle manipulation on thin-liquidity collateral
TypedRisks.description: After the 117 million USD Mango Markets exploit, Compound governance paused YFI, ZRX, BAT and MKR as collateral because their spot liquidity was too thin to resist price manipulation. Manipulable collateral lets an attacker borrow far more than the asset is worth.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Collateral pausing for the four assets, passed with 99 percent support
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: On-chain DEX depth for each collateral asset versus the maximum borrow it can support
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: Cointelegraph on Compound pausing four tokens

TypedRisks.name: Oracle price diverging from tradeable market price on yield-bearing stables
TypedRisks.description: During the Elixir liquidity crunch the sdeUSD oracle reported 1.06 while the market price was 0.86, letting a borrower draw 1.06 times an 88 percent LTV, or about 0.93 USD of value per 0.86 USD of collateral. Gauntlet described this as a vulnerability.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Emergency withdraw-pause on the Ethereum USDC, USDS and USDT comets, keeping supply and repay open while blocking borrow and withdraw
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Oracle price minus secondary market price for every yield-bearing collateral, alerting above a fixed basis point gap

TypedRisks.name: Collateral issuer failure
TypedRisks.description: Elixir's deUSD and sdeUSD were listed as collateral on three Ethereum comets when the issuer hit a liquidity crunch. The protocol had no way to exit the exposure without pausing markets that also held unrelated collateral.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Emergency pause and subsequent removal from collateral sets
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Issuer redemption queue length and reserve attestation freshness for every synthetic stablecoin collateral

TypedRisks.name: Whale governance capture of the treasury
TypedRisks.description: Proposal 289, led by the whale Humpy and The Golden Boys, passed and would have automatically deployed 24 million USD of treasury funds into a goldCOMP product. The vote succeeded despite broad community objection.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Negotiated truce, proposal withdrawal and cancellation of the deployment, plus a replacement staking product endorsed by OpenZeppelin and Gauntlet
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Voting power concentration in the top wallets versus the quorum threshold, and any proposal that moves treasury funds automatically on execution
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: The Block on the Compound truce with Humpy

TypedRisks.name: Coarse pause granularity in v3
TypedRisks.description: The v4 roadmap concedes that v3's governance lacked fine-tuned risk controls and that during the Elixir event the team needed to pause all markets. A single bad collateral forces an outage across every user of that comet.
TypedRisks.mitigation: v4 design adds isolated margin assets, asset-level caps and pauses, and a third-party risk manager
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Number of assets affected per pause action relative to the number actually impaired

TypedRisks.name: Liquidation absorption cost during a crash
TypedRisks.description: The 10 October 2025 crash produced 438 liquidations with BTC down over 12 percent and ETH down over 20 percent, from 4,354 to 3,435 USD. Compound paid 40.65 million USD in absorption payouts, the largest being 15.4 million USD or 38 percent on V3 Ethereum USDC.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Absorption mechanism worked as designed and about 1.49 million USD was added to reserves
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Absorption payout total per 24 hours and reserve balance change per comet

TypedRisks.name: Residual bad debt on low-liquidity chains
TypedRisks.description: The 10 October 2025 crash left under 1,600 USD of bad debt, mostly on Unichain. Small deployments have thinner liquidator coverage than mainnet.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Recommendation to deprecate the Ronin Comet, and continued monitoring of small chain deployments
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Bad debt balance per chain and liquidator bot participation rate on non-mainnet comets

TypedRisks.name: Multi-chain deployment sprawl
TypedRisks.description: Compound runs comets across multiple chains including Unichain and Ronin, and Gauntlet has recommended deprecating the Ronin Comet. Each additional deployment adds monitoring and liquidator coverage obligations without proportionate revenue.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Active deprecation recommendations for underused comets
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Utilisation and revenue per comet versus the risk monitoring cost of maintaining it

TypedRisks.name: Exchange-sourced oracle divergence triggering mass liquidations
TypedRisks.description: On 26 November 2020 the DAI price spiked to 1.30 USD on Coinbase Pro, which the oracle passed through, and 85.2 million USD of DAI positions were liquidated. Users were liquidated on a price that did not reflect broad market conditions.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Later oracle stack combines Chainlink feeds with Uniswap anchors, which bounds single-venue divergence
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Spread between the oracle source venue price and the volume-weighted cross-venue price for every stablecoin
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: Compound forum proposal on DAI liquidation compensation

TypedRisks.name: No reliable remediation path for harmed users
TypedRisks.description: The compensation proposal for the November 2020 DAI liquidations failed an executive vote, with 680,000 COMP against and 212,000 COMP for. Users harmed by a protocol-level pricing failure have no guaranteed recourse.
TypedRisks.mitigation: None documented beyond ad hoc governance proposals
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Outcome and vote margin of any remediation proposal following a protocol-caused loss
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: Compound forum proposal on DAI liquidation compensation

TypedRisks.name: Liquid staking and restaking token depeg
TypedRisks.description: During the 10 October 2025 crash, rsETH, weETH and wstETH tracked ETH with no meaningful depeg. The exposure remains because these assets rely on redemption mechanics that are untested at maximum stress.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Continued Gauntlet monitoring and per-asset caps
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Secondary market price of each LST and LRT versus its redemption rate, alerting on a sustained discount

TypedRisks.name: Dependence on a Chainlink and Uniswap oracle stack
TypedRisks.description: The oracle stack combines Chainlink feeds with Uniswap anchors, so a failure or manipulation of either component propagates into every market price. The 2022 cETH incident showed how a single oracle contract change can freeze a market outright.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Anchor design bounds single-source manipulation, and v4 proposes a next-generation oracle design
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Chainlink feed staleness above the configured heartbeat, and Uniswap anchor deviation beyond the allowed band

TypedRisks.name: Permissioned and KYC market design
TypedRisks.description: The v4 roadmap includes permissioned and KYC vaults for institutions alongside the open markets. Introducing identity gating creates compliance obligations and a two-tier user base inside one protocol.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Separation of permissioned vaults from open markets in the v4 architecture
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Share of TVL sitting in permissioned vaults and any change to their access criteria

Proposal 119 executed at 01:18 UTC on 7 September 2022 and restored the feed; OpenZeppelin published a post-mortem and no direct loss occurred.
Following the 117 million USD Mango Markets exploit, Compound governance paused YFI, ZRX, BAT and MKR as collateral over price manipulation risk.
The proposal passed with 99 percent support and the four assets were removed from active collateral use.
Proposal 289, led by the whale Humpy and The Golden Boys, passed and would have automatically deployed 24 million USD of treasury funds into a goldCOMP product on execution.
A truce was reached, the proposal was withdrawn and the deployment was cancelled; a replacement staking product endorsed by OpenZeppelin and Gauntlet was pursued instead.
A market-wide crash with BTC down over 12 percent and ETH down over 20 percent, from 4,354 to 3,435 USD, produced 438 liquidations across Compound comets.
V3 Ethereum USDC absorbed the largest share at 15.4 million USD or 38 percent; bad debt stayed under 1,600 USD, mostly on Unichain, and about 1.49 million USD was added to reserves.
An Elixir liquidity crunch hit deUSD and sdeUSD, which were listed as collateral on the Ethereum USDC, USDS and USDT comets; the sdeUSD oracle showed 1.06 while the market price was 0.86.
Gauntlet triggered an emergency withdraw-pause, keeping supply and repay open while blocking borrow and withdraw, and characterised the oracle gap as a vulnerability.

compound.RiskPosture: Compound's history is dominated by oracle and governance failures rather than direct contract exploits, and the pattern is remarkably consistent across six years. The November 2020 DAI liquidations, the 2022 cETH feed freeze and the November 2025 Elixir sdeUSD gap are all the same failure class: the protocol's internal price diverged from the tradeable price and the system acted on the wrong number ([Compound forum](https://www.comp.xyz/t/proposal-distribute-dai-to-users-affected-by-dai-liquidations/2110), [OpenZeppelin post-mortem](https://www.comp.xyz/t/ceth-price-feed-incident-post-mortem/3578), [Gauntlet](https://www.comp.xyz/t/gauntlet-pausing-ethereum-usdc-usds-and-usdt-comets/7326)). On the governance side, both the 2021 reward distribution bug and the 2024 Humpy treasury proposal show that executable code can reach production with insufficient review or insufficient community control ([CryptoSlate](https://cryptoslate.com/how-the-tiniest-of-errors-resulted-in-an-80-million-loss-for-compound-finance/), [The Block](https://www.theblock.co/post/308215/compound-reaches-truce-with-crypto-whale-humpy-after-controversial-vote-to-move-24-million-in-tokens)). The offsetting strength is that core solvency has been robust: the October 2025 crash produced 438 liquidations and under 1,600 USD of bad debt ([Gauntlet](https://www.comp.xyz/t/gauntlet-compound-market-downturn-analysis-10-10-2025/7297)). The team itself has named the structural weakness, that v3 forces all-or-nothing pauses, and the v4 roadmap is an explicit response with isolated margin assets, asset-level pauses and a new oracle design ([Compound v4 roadmap](https://www.comp.xyz/t/recreating-compound-v4-platform-roadmap/7529)). Net posture: medium severity, oracle and governance driven, with credible remediation in flight but not yet shipped.

morpho.name: Morpho
morpho.AssetStrategy: Asset strategy. Morpho has no protocol level asset list at all. Anyone can deploy an immutable market defined by a collateral token, a loan token, an LLTV and an oracle, so "supported assets" means whichever markets curators and vaults have actually funded. There are no supply or borrow caps at the market level; exposure limits live in the ERC-4626 vaults that allocate into markets. Liquidation incentive is derived from LLTV rather than set per asset, and [the Morpho liquidation documentation](https://docs.morpho.org/build/borrow/concepts/liquidation/) states that at an LLTV of 86 percent the liquidation incentive factor is approximately 1.05, a 5 percent bonus, with the protocol taking no fee; Morpho does not publish the general formula on that page, so bonuses at other LLTVs are marked n.a. below. The practical consequence is that Morpho's Ethereum book is dominated by a handful of LLTV tiers (86, 91.5, 94.5, 96.5 percent) and by long tail collateral that no shared pool would list: tokenised credit tranches, Pendle principal tokens, RWA style yield tokens and curator specific dollars. TypedRisks.name: Unlicensed curators making unilateral risk decisions
TypedRisks.description: Curator TVL grew from 300 million USD to 7 billion USD, a 2,200 percent increase, with the top five curators holding roughly 43 percent share and no major curator licensed. Depositors delegate credit decisions to entities with no regulatory obligation and no capital at risk.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Role separation into Owner, Curator, Allocator and Sentinel, timelocks, abdication, gates, adapter registry and fee caps of 50 percent performance and 5 percent management
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Curator AUM concentration, and the delay between a new market listing and its first published risk rationale
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: Chorus One on DeFi curators in 2025

TypedRisks.name: Hardcoded oracle prices blocking liquidation
TypedRisks.description: Stream Finance vault oracles hardcoded xUSD near one dollar, so when the token collapsed liquidations could not trigger and utilisation hit 100 percent. Bad debt ran into the hundreds of millions across at least fifteen Morpho vaults plus Euler.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Post-incident scrutiny of hardcoded and rate-based oracles, and market close-only settings
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Any market where the oracle is a fixed constant or an internal exchange rate rather than a market-derived price

TypedRisks.name: Donation-based inflation attack with a faulty oracle
TypedRisks.description: Morpho's own documentation warns that on Vaults V1 an attacker can donate into a market with a mispriced oracle and inflict losses on the vault, and that supply caps do not protect against this. A market sitting in the withdrawal queue with a cap of zero is still vulnerable and the loss is unbounded by the cap.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Documented warning, adapter registry, and guidance to remove markets entirely rather than only zeroing caps
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Any vault holding a market with a non-market oracle, and unexpected share balance increases in a vault it did not initiate

TypedRisks.name: LP-token oracle manipulation via flash loan
TypedRisks.description: The Aerodrome sAMM-cUSDO/USDC LP oracle read raw pool reserves combined with a Chainlink USDC feed, a cUSDO ERC-4626 rate and a hardcoded one dollar USDO price. An attacker flash-loaned 6,666,666.67 USDC, inflated the LP value, borrowed 363,935 USDC and self-liquidated.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Market set to close-only with allocations zeroed, and the curator fully compensated the 49,303.14 USDC of bad debt
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Any oracle that reads spot AMM reserves, and any collateral whose price includes a hardcoded stablecoin leg

TypedRisks.name: Last-depositor bank run in Vaults V1.1
TypedRisks.description: Morpho documents that in Vault V1.1 the last depositor to exit bears the bad debt left in the vault. This creates a rational incentive to withdraw first at the earliest sign of trouble.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Documented explicitly, plus Sentinel role and timelocks to slow adverse changes
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Withdrawal velocity relative to vault liquidity, and any vault where realised bad debt is not yet socialised

TypedRisks.name: Adapter removal frontrunning
TypedRisks.description: Removing an adapter without first setting its caps to zero can be frontrun, letting an attacker act between the two operations. This is an operational sequencing hazard rather than a code defect.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Documented requirement to zero caps before calling removeAdapter
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Any removeAdapter transaction not preceded by a cap-zeroing transaction in the same block sequence

TypedRisks.name: Reverting oracle putting a market into a degraded state
TypedRisks.description: If an oracle reverts, borrow and liquidate calls revert with it, leaving a market that cannot be de-risked. Positions become frozen at whatever health factor they held at the moment of failure.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Documented degraded-state behaviour so curators can plan a fallback
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Oracle call revert rate per market, and time since the last successful price update

TypedRisks.name: Curator and venue concentration
TypedRisks.description: The top three curators, Steakhouse, Sentora and Gauntlet, together managed about 5.14 billion USD, and Morpho was the largest single venue at 2.91 billion USD. A single curator's error propagates across a large share of the deposit base.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Vault-level isolation and per-vault caps, plus public curator dashboards
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Share of protocol TVL controlled by the top three curators, and overlap of the same collateral across their vaults

TypedRisks.name: Withdrawal queuing and rate spikes during stress
TypedRisks.description: During the Stream Finance fallout withdrawals were queued and rates spiked as high as 190 percent, with 80 percent of withdrawals completing within three days. Even Steakhouse and Gauntlet USDC vaults that had no xUSD exposure became briefly illiquid.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Interest rate curves that price scarcity, and withdrawal queues that avoid a disorderly first-mover race
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Vault utilisation at or near 100 percent, and the length of the withdrawal queue in hours
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: Chorus One on DeFi curators in 2025

TypedRisks.name: Curator discretion used against borrowers
TypedRisks.description: In the PT-USD0++ / USDC vault, users complained that curators cut the supply allocation to 20 million USD and drove rates to three figures for up to 30 hours, which they characterised as punitive. The curator justified it by an imbalanced Pendle SY/PT pool that limited liquidation capacity.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Public forum disclosure of curator rationale, and Morpho's documented role and timelock framework
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Sudden allocation cuts and borrow rate jumps in a vault with no corresponding collateral price move
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: Morpho forum thread on PT-USD0++ vault curators

TypedRisks.name: Public Allocator enabling cross-vault contagion
TypedRisks.description: After the Resolv exploit, 6.2 million USD of bad debt reached Morpho vaults via the Public Allocator, with Gauntlet accounting for 96 percent of the total losses. Morpho's supply() accepts an onBehalf parameter, so anyone can credit market shares to a vault without its authorisation.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Curators setting supply caps to zero on affected markets, and a compensation plan announced
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Inbound supply() calls naming a vault as onBehalf that the vault did not initiate
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: Oak Research on the Resolv USR hack

TypedRisks.name: Over-reliance on third-party risk endorsements
TypedRisks.description: Steakhouse Financial published a report five days before the Resolv hack calling the protocol institutionally rigorous and crisis-ready, and other curators used it to justify exposure. Steakhouse itself had no direct USR exposure while the curators relying on its work took the losses.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Public post-incident scrutiny and calls for higher due diligence, real-time monitoring and built-in circuit breakers
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Whether a curator's allocation rationale rests on its own analysis or on another party's published report
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: Oak Research on the Resolv USR hack

TypedRisks.name: Immutable core with no parameter correction path
TypedRisks.description: Morpho's core is immutable and the LLTV of a market cannot be changed once created. A market created with an unsafe LLTV or oracle can only be abandoned, never fixed.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Immutability audited by Certora formal verification, with a Cantina bug bounty of 2,500,000 USD
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Number of live markets flagged as unsafe that remain listed because they cannot be reparameterised

TypedRisks.name: Front-end and SDK misconfiguration routing approvals
TypedRisks.description: On 10 April 2025 a front-end and SDK misconfiguration sent token approvals to the Bundler3 contract instead of the intended adapters. One user's bundled transaction was intercepted, though by a whitehat MEV bot rather than an attacker.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Rollback within four minutes, contracts themselves unaffected, public incident write-up
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Approval targets in front-end transactions diverging from the canonical adapter address list

TypedRisks.name: Vault shares used as collateral
TypedRisks.description: Morpho documentation states that Vault V1.0 is not recommended for use as collateral. Recursive use of vault shares stacks oracle, bad debt and liquidity risk from the underlying markets into a single collateral token.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Explicit documentation warning, and the V1.1 revision

morpho.RiskPosture: Morpho has almost no protocol-level risk and almost all of its risk in the layer above it. The immutable core is formally verified by Certora with a 2.5 million USD Cantina bounty ([Morpho docs](https://docs.morpho.org/learn/resources/risks/)), and in three documented loss events the core behaved exactly as specified. The damage came from curators: who they listed, what oracles they accepted and how fast they reacted. Every major loss traces to a collateral issuer failing while an oracle told the market nothing was wrong, in the Aerodrome LP case ([ClearstarLabs](https://forum.morpho.org/t/post-mortem-aerodrome-cusdo-usdc-amm-lp-oracle-manipulation-on-morpho-lending-market/1794)), in Stream's hardcoded xUSD price ([TokenIntel](https://tokenintel.org/reports/stream-finance-post-mortem-2026-05-21.html)) and in Resolv's hardcoded USR oracle exploited through the Public Allocator ([Oak Research](https://oakresearch.io/en/analyses/investigations/the-resolv-usr-hack-curators-face-their-responsibilities)). Morpho's own documentation is unusually candid about the residual hazards, including donation attacks that supply caps do not stop and the last-depositor bank run in Vaults V1.1 ([Morpho security considerations](https://docs.morpho.org/curate/concepts/security-considerations/)). The structural problem is that curator TVL grew 2,200 percent to 7 billion USD with no licensing and heavy concentration in five firms ([Chorus One](https://chorus.one/reports-research/defi-curators-in-2025-navigating-chaos-building-resilience)). Net posture: low technological risk in the base layer, critical and recurring counterparty and governance risk in the curated layer, with loss magnitude driven almost entirely by curator judgement.

A new native USDC market on Arbitrum launched with empty reserves; the attacker manipulated liquidityIndex through repeated flash loans combined with rounding in favour of the user on rToken burn, and borrowed 1900 WETH.

Remediation proceeded with US law enforcement and ZeroShadow; multisigs were tightened to 4-of-7 with a minimum 72-hour timelock on upgrades and ownership transfers, and a full Aave V2 Lending Suite redeployment was planned.

The DAO began an orderly wind-down after eighteen months of failing to recover exploited funds, secure financing or restore growth; active development ceased immediately.

radiant.RiskPosture: Radiant is no longer a going concern and its risk profile should be read as exit risk, not lending risk. Two exploits inside ten months, a roughly 720 ETH shortfall from a flash loan against an empty new market in January 2024 ([Radiant post-mortem](https://medium.com/@RadiantCapital/post-mortem-report-radiant-capital-aea46cb985ae)) and about 50 million USD from a device-malware multisig compromise in October 2024 ([Radiant post-mortem](https://medium.com/@RadiantCapital/radiant-post-mortem-fecd6cd38081)), destroyed the protocol's capital base and its trust. Neither loss was recovered, and after eighteen months with no external investment and no grants the DAO began an orderly wind-down on 1 June 2026 ([WuBlockchain](https://www.wublockchain.xyz/news/radiant-capital-wind-down-after-50m-exploit-failure-19380)). The dominant risks now are operational rather than financial: borrowing is disabled with caps at 1, RDNT emissions have stopped, support is best-effort, the front-end only survives through end of year, and the DAO explicitly warns that no further upgrades, patches or interventions should be assumed ([Sunsetting Radiant Capital DAO](https://medium.com/@RadiantCapital/sunsetting-radiant-capital-dao-entering-recovery-phase-and-lessons-for-the-future-of-defi-c47837ffa499)). Some RIZ vault losses were declared permanently irrecoverable ([RIZ post-mortem](https://community.radiant.capital/t/post-mortem-october-16-2024-exploit-impact-on-riz-vaults/2220)). Net posture: critical, terminal, and the only rational user action is capital withdrawal, which is exactly what the DAO itself advises.

spark.name: Spark Protocol
spark.AssetStrategy:
Asset strategy. Spark is the Sky (formerly MakerDAO) lending arm and its coverage is two different things at once. SparkLend is a deliberately short Aave v3 style collateral list: 18 reserves on Ethereum, of which only WETH, wstETH, WBTC, cbBTC, LBTC and weETH carry a non zero loan to value, while the dollar assets (USDC, USDT, USDS, PYUSD) are configured as pure borrow assets with LTV and liquidation threshold at zero and effectively unlimited caps. [The SparkLend documentation](https://docs.spark.fi/products/sparklend) is explicit that the list is short by design, that ETH e-mode collateral is limited to wstETH and rETH, and that BTC e-mode was removed entirely. The second and larger half of Spark's asset coverage is allocation driven rather than collateral driven: the [Spark Liquidity Layer](https://docs.spark.fi/products/spark-liquidity-layer) moves USDS, USDC and USDT into Sky's PSM, Aave v3 and SparkLend, Spark curated Morpho vaults, Curve and Uniswap stablecoin pools, Ethena USDe and sUSDe, EtherFi weETH, Lido wstETH, Maple redemptions, Superstate USTB and OTC desks across Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Unichain, Avalanche and Robinhood Chain, all under keccak256 keyed rate limits with a max amount and a refill slope, and any unapproved venue reverts. Spark Savings adds ERC-4626 vaults (spUSDC, spUSDT, spPYUSD, spETH, spUSDG, plus Sky's sUSDS and stUSDS) whose exposure is again allocation rather than collateral, per [the Spark Savings documentation](https://docs.spark.fi/products/spark-savings). So a reader comparing Spark to Aave on collateral lists alone will badly understate its asset footprint.

SparkLend Ethereum, Pool `0xC13e21B648A5Ee794902342038FF3aDAB66BE987` and AaveOracle `0x8105f69D9C41644c6A0803fDA7D03Aa70996cFD9`, both from the [Spark address registry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sparkdotfi/spark-address-registry/master/src/SparkLend.sol). All 18 reserves are shown.

spark.RiskPosture: Spark's posture is deliberately conservative on the lending side and aggressive on the balance sheet side, and the two must be assessed separately. SparkLend itself is a hardened Aave v3 fork with a three-oracle median across RedStone, Chainlink and Chronicle, a killswitch peg-ratio oracle, rate-limited caps and a tight collateral set that excludes BTC e-mode entirely ([SparkLend docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/sparklend)). That conservatism paid off when the January 2026 deprecation spell froze rsETH three months before the Kelp exploit, leaving Spark with no direct exposure and attracting 1.4 billion USD of fleeing Aave deposits ([Sky executive vote](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sky-ecosystem/executive-votes/main/2026/executive-vote-2026-01-29-msc-pattern-and-skybase-onboarding.md), [Streetbrief](https://www.streetbrief.co/article/spark-protocol-captures-1-4b-inflow-kelp-dao-exploit-triggers-aave-liquidity-crisis-2604/)). The real risk sits in the Spark Liquidity Layer, which allocates up to 1.1 billion USD directly to Ethena's USDe and sUSDe plus 200 million DAI to Pendle PT markets ([Spark mirror post](https://mirror.xyz/0xF99d0E4E3435cc9C9868D1C6274DfaB3e2721341/LjBAybIk6-waSxwOBWp5mg_37jNvrWF_UdzqqXoEl6U)) and routes capital across CCTP, LayerZero, Maple and Superstate via a relayer whose own threat model assumes it can be fully compromised ([SLL docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/spark-liquidity-layer)). Loss absorption is unusually deep, six layers ending in SKY token issuance and equal socialisation across USDS holders ([Spark Savings docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/spark-savings)), but that final layer means Spark depositors are ultimately Sky creditors. Net posture: low protocol risk, concentrated issuer and operational risk on the treasury side, with the strongest incident record of the five.

extra-finance.name: Extra Finance
extra-finance.AssetStrategy: Extra Finance runs two distinct products with two completely different asset surfaces. The older one is leveraged yield farming (LYF), where the "supported asset" is not a single token but an AMM LP pool on Velodrome (Optimism) or Aerodrome (Base): the user deposits one or both pool tokens, borrows the pool tokens from Extra's lending reserves, and the protocol mints an LP position that is auto-compounded. Risk is expressed per farming vault as a Liquidation Threshold stated as a maximum Debt Ratio plus a maximum leverage multiple, not as a per-token LTV, and every farming vault has its own numeric Vault ID ([Extra Finance Pool Info](https://docs.extrafi.io/extra_finance/leverage-farming/pool-info)). The second product is XLend, an Aave v3 fork on Base and Optimism with conventional per-reserve LTV, liquidation threshold, liquidation bonus, supply cap, borrow cap, E-Mode and isolation-mode debt ceilings ([XLend E-Mode docs](https://docs.extrafi.io/extrafi-xlend/borrow-lend/e-mode), [XLend Isolation Mode docs](https://docs.extrafi.io/extrafi-xlend/borrow-lend/isolation-mode)). What distinguishes Extra is the split oracle philosophy between the two: LYF prices positions off the AMM curve itself with a TWAP and a Chainlink deviation guard, while XLend uses Chainlink as primary ([Extra Finance Price Feed](https://docs.extrafi.io/extra_finance/leverage-farming/price-feed), [XLend Price Feed](https://docs.extrafi.io/extrafi-xlend/borrow-lend/price-feed)). The XLend docs "Parameters" page is published but empty, so all XLend numbers below were read directly from the on-chain Aave v3 `Pool.getConfiguration(address)` reserve configuration bitmap on Base pool `0x09b11746dfd1b5a8325e30943f8b3d5000922e03` and Optimism pool `0x345D2827f36621b02B783f7D5004B4a2fec00186` on 2026-07-26, the Optimism pool address being the one published by Extra ([Extra Finance contracts](https://docs.extrafi.io/extra_finance/contracts-and-transparency)). TypedRisks.name: Oracle manipulation of the 30-minute TWAP

TypedRisks.mitigation: TWAP is aggregated with a Chainlink price feed for pricing, and leverage is capped for low-credibility assets.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Divergence between the on-chain TWAP and the Chainlink reference feed for each listed asset.

TypedRisks.name: Liquidation bot failure creating bad debt
TypedRisks.description: The docs state directly that if the liquidation bot fails to close a leveraged position in time there would be bad debt. The team initially operates the bot itself for LYF positions.
TypedRisks.mitigation: XLend liquidations are permissionless with a health factor below 1 trigger, which removes single-operator dependency on that product.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Count of positions sitting above the liquidation threshold for more than one block interval.

TypedRisks.name: Realised bad debt from a collateral asset collapse
TypedRisks.description: In February 2025 the protocol suffered bad debt on EXA and the community had to pass an emergency response proposal. Loss size was not disclosed in the monthly review.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Governance emergency response process; asset isolation and per-asset supply, borrow and LTV caps in XLend.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: New governance proposals tagged as emergency response, and reserve or bad debt line items per lending pool.

TypedRisks.name: Recursive looping and self-referential liquidity
TypedRisks.description: Leverage supplied by Extra Finance can become a large share of the liquidity in the very pool being farmed, so a forced unwind moves the price against itself. Extra Finance says it may temporarily disable leverage on new positions when its own share of a pool exceeds roughly 30%.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Explicit 30% liquidity proportion trigger that disables new leveraged positions in that pool.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Extra Finance share of total liquidity in each farmed DEX pool.

TypedRisks.name: Lender withdrawal blocked at high utilization
TypedRisks.description: If the utilization rate of a lending pool is very high, lenders may be unable to withdraw on time until farmers repay. This is a structural feature of the shared lending pool design.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Interest rate curve rises with utilization to draw repayment and new supply.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Utilization rate per lending pool, especially sustained readings above 90%.

TypedRisks.name: Chain concentration on Base and Optimism
TypedRisks.description: Effectively all TVL sits on two OP Stack chains: Base $22.76m and OP Mainnet $1.65m, with only $10.83 on Berachain. A sequencer halt, reorg or bridge failure on Base would freeze the majority of the book, including liquidations.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Deployment across more than one Superchain chain, though both share the OP Stack codebase.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Base and Optimism sequencer uptime and L2 block production; bridge withdrawal queue length.

TypedRisks.name: TVL contraction and franchise decay
TypedRisks.description: TVL fell from $116.79m in August 2024 to $79.78m at end of February 2025 to $24.41m at time of research. Shrinking deposits reduce fee revenue and thin out the liquidity that makes liquidation safe.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Incentive programs including Optimism OP rounds and EXTRA emissions.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Monthly TVL by chain and by product (LYF versus XLend).

TypedRisks.name: Governance token illiquidity
TypedRisks.description: Total EXTRA on-chain liquidity is $713,613, concentrated in Aerodrome V1 at $605,284. Any treasury or incentive sale, or a governance attack requiring token accumulation, interacts with a very shallow market.
TypedRisks.mitigation: EXTRA token owner role has been invalidated so no new mints are possible; 2.25% of protocol fees are burned weekly.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: EXTRA DEX liquidity depth and 2% slippage size.

TypedRisks.name: Lapsed real-time threat monitoring
TypedRisks.description: The Hexagate monitoring partnership was "not yet renewed in 2025, still in review" as of the docs page. Without an active monitoring vendor, detection of an in-progress exploit relies on the team alone.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Immunefi bug bounty with maximum bounty $100,000 remains live; audits by BlockSec, PeckShield and Sherlock.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Public confirmation of a renewed monitoring vendor contract.

TypedRisks.name: Smart contract risk on a large audited surface
TypedRisks.description: The bounty scope covers XAccount factories and a full Aave-style lending market (Pool, PoolConfigurator, ACL_Manager, A_Token, Debt_Token), a wide attack surface for a small team. Oracle manipulation and flash loan attacks are explicitly in scope, meaning they are recognised as live threats.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Three audits (BlockSec, PeckShield, Sherlock December 2024); no admin function to withdraw user funds; multisig-gated configuration.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: New critical or high severity bounty payouts, and unaudited contract deployments.

TypedRisks.name: Multisig configuration authority
TypedRisks.description: Protocol configuration is controlled by a multisig, and risk parameters such as leverage caps and liquidation thresholds are set administratively rather than by a slow on-chain vote. Mis-set parameters or key compromise would directly change solvency.
TypedRisks.mitigation: No admin function exists to withdraw user funds; parameter changes are documented as subject to governance procedures.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Multisig signer set changes and parameter change transactions.

TypedRisks.name: Cross-chain token bridge dependency
TypedRisks.description: EXTRA is bridged between chains using a LayerZero OFT implementation. A messaging layer failure would break EXTRA fungibility across the Superchain deployments.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Single canonical OFT implementation rather than multiple wrapped representations.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: LayerZero endpoint incidents and EXTRA supply reconciliation across chains.

TypedRisks.name: Insurance cover reliance
TypedRisks.description: Coverage is offered through third-party providers OpenCover and InsurAce rather than an internal protocol-owned backstop. Payout depends on those providers' own solvency and claims assessment.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Optional external cover available to users; protocol-level reserves not documented.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Available cover capacity and premium pricing on OpenCover and InsurAce for Extra Finance.

extra-finance.RiskPosture: Extra Finance is a small and shrinking leveraged farming protocol whose risk is concentrated rather than systemic. The design is conservative in places: partial liquidation at 30% of a position, an 8% fee on only the liquidated slice, per-asset caps in XLend, no admin withdrawal function and a self-imposed rule to disable leverage when its own liquidity share of a farmed pool exceeds about 30%. Against that, the protocol depends on a team-operated liquidation bot for the farming product, on a 30-minute on-chain TWAP that is manipulable in shallow markets, and on two OP Stack chains for essentially all of its book. The February 2025 EXA bad debt event shows the failure mode is real, and the collapse in TVL from roughly $117m in August 2024 to about $24m today means both revenue and the liquidity cushion that keeps liquidations orderly are much thinner than when the parameters were designed.

fluid.name: Fluid
fluid.AssetStrategy:
Fluid's core innovation is that a vault is the unit of listing, not a token, and both sides of a vault can be a DEX position rather than a plain ERC-20. In classic Fluid vaults the collateral token and the debt token are ordinary assets, but in smart collateral vaults the deposit is an LP share of a Fluid DEX pool, and in smart debt vaults the borrowing itself is a DEX position so the borrower earns trading fees on the debt leg while paying borrow interest. Vault 44 on Ethereum, wstETH-ETH collateral against wstETH-ETH debt, is smart collateral plus smart debt at once, and vault 51, WBTC-cbBTC against WBTC-cbBTC, is the BTC analogue. This means "supported asset" for Fluid has to be read as an ordered pair plus a mode, and the same underlying token can appear with materially different collateral factors depending on the pairing. Fluid also runs a dual-oracle design where the price used to permit an operation can differ from the price used to permit a liquidation, and vault upgrades are shipped by deploying new vault versions and winding down the old ones over months rather than by mutating parameters in place ([Fluid governance, Deploy Fluid upgrades to Vault protocol](https://gov.fluid.io/t/deploy-fluid-upgrades-to-vault-protocol/764), [MixBytes analysis of the Fluid vault](https://mixbytes.io/blog/modern-defi-lending-protocols-how-its-made-fluid-vault)). Every parameter row below was read live on 2026-07-26 from the Fluid public vault API for each chain, for example [api.fluid.instadapp.io/v2/1/vaults](https://api.fluid.instadapp.io/v2/1/vaults). Protocol TVL is roughly $797M ([DefiLlama Fluid](https://defillama.com/protocol/fluid)).

Column mapping for Fluid: "Max LTV %" is the vault `collateralFactor`, "Liq. threshold %" is `liquidationThreshold`, "Liq. bonus %" is `liquidationPenalty`, "Supply cap" is the liquidity layer `baseWithdrawalLimit` in collateral-token units, and "Borrow cap" is `maxBorrowLimit` in debt-token units. Fluid additionally publishes a `liquidationMaxLimit` (LML), the hard ceiling above which a position can be fully liquidated, which is reported in Notes.

TypedRisks.name: Looping concentration in yield-bearing stablecoin wrappers
TypedRisks.description: Roughly 98% of wstUSR supply sat inside Fluid leverage loops at up to 6x when USR broke, giving ~$100m exposure to a single wrapper that was 18.9% of all-chain lending TVL. The current book repeats the shape: SUSDAI 19.9%, WSTETH 16.8%, WEETH 12.9%, REUSD 12.7%, WBTC 6.8%, top five 69.0%.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Isolated vault design with per-vault parameters; May 2026 oracle upgrades added token classification and legal agreements with asset issuers.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Share of a wrapper's total supply held inside Fluid vaults, and top-five collateral concentration as a percentage of lending TVL.

TypedRisks.name: Collateral issuer key compromise leading to bad debt
TypedRisks.description: On 22 March 2026 a compromised Resolv Labs AWS KMS SERVICE_ROLE key allowed ~80m unbacked USR to be minted for ~$200k of USDC, and USR fell from $1.00 to $0.0025 on Curve. Fluid absorbed roughly $10m to $21m of bad debt as a result.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Bad debt was covered 100% by discretionary off-balance-sheet loans, and a $19.3m settlement was agreed in May 2026 split across Resolv, the Fluid treasury and the Fluid team.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Issuer operational security disclosures, and any unexplained expansion in a collateral token's supply relative to attested reserves.

TypedRisks.name: Bridged LRT collateral exploit
TypedRisks.description: On 18 April 2026 about 116,500 rsETH, roughly 18% of supply and ~$292m, was drained through a LayerZero cross-chain messaging exploit at Kelp DAO. Fluid TVL fell from $1.04b to $861m, a 17.5% drop over two days.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Fluid froze rsETH markets within hours, alongside Aave, SparkLend and Upshift; no bad debt resulted.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Supply reconciliation for bridged LRTs across chains, and LayerZero endpoint incident feeds.

TypedRisks.name: Bank run risk from shared liquidity layer
TypedRisks.description: All products draw on one Liquidity Layer, so a shock in one collateral drains liquidity available to every other market. The Resolv event produced ~$300m of net outflows in a single day and a 30.3% TVL fall in 24 hours.
TypedRisks.mitigation: fToken exchange rates are monotonically increasing so lenders did not realise losses on Ethereum; utilization-linked rate curve (USDC kink1 85% at 5.40%, kink2 93% at 7.50%, max 40%).
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Single-day net outflow as a percentage of TVL, and Liquidity Layer free liquidity.

TypedRisks.name: Sustained very high utilization blocking withdrawals
TypedRisks.description: Several markets run near their ceiling: BNB USDT 96.7%, Polygon USDT0 92.1%, Plasma USDT0 90.9%, Arbitrum USDC 90.3%, Ethereum GHO 86.7% and ETH 84.9%. At these levels lenders cannot exit at scale without a rate spike forcing repayment.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Two-kink rate model with a 40% maximum rate on USDC to force deleveraging past kink2 at 93%.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Utilization by asset and chain, and time spent above kink2.

TypedRisks.name: Thin liquidation buffers on high-LTV correlated pairs
TypedRisks.description: LTVs run from 80% to 95% and the liquidation penalty can be as low as 0.1% for correlated pairs such as wstETH/ETH. A 0.1% penalty gives liquidators almost no margin for gas and slippage in a fast market.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Tick-based liquidation engine designed for high throughput at low penalty; per-vault parameterisation.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Realised liquidation shortfall versus penalty collected, and liquidator participation count per event.

TypedRisks.name: Modular oracle configuration error
TypedRisks.description: Oracles are configured per vault and mix Chainlink, Uniswap V3 TWAP, Redstone and custom center-price oracles. Heterogeneous per-vault wiring means a single misconfigured feed can mispricing an entire market.
TypedRisks.mitigation: May 2026 oracle upgrade added per-key pricing, multi-source feeds and deviation checks.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Per-vault oracle deviation alerts and feed staleness.

TypedRisks.name: One-day governance timelock
TypedRisks.description: The GovernorBravo timelock at 0x2386DC45AdDed673317eF068992F19421B481F4c enforces only an 86,400 second delay, with a 4,000,000 FLUID quorum and 1,000,000 FLUID proposal threshold. A single day gives lenders almost no time to exit ahead of a hostile or mistaken parameter change.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Guardian Avocado multisig 0x4F6F977aCDD1177DCD81aB83074855EcB9C2D49e operating 7-of-14 can pause but cannot increase risk.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Queued proposals in the timelock and FLUID voting-power concentration.

TypedRisks.name: Discretionary treasury and multisig action outside governance
TypedRisks.description: A team multisig drew roughly $8m of USDC and USDT from the shared liquidity layer via a pre-approved credit line before the governance vote on the bad debt, and the proposal to move fGHO and iETHv2 from treasury to a team multisig drew public criticism including from Curve founder Michael Egorov. Critics argued it altered the risk exposure of USDC and USDT depositors.
TypedRisks.mitigation: The action was subsequently put to governance and disclosed publicly; a formal settlement was agreed in May 2026.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Pre-approved credit line draws by non-governance multisigs, and treasury asset transfers.

TypedRisks.name: Operational key compromise on peripheral systems
TypedRisks.description: On 1 June 2026 the Ethereum reward distribution system was exploited for about $215,000 through compromised operational keys rather than a contract flaw, with proceeds swapped to ETH and laundered through Tornado Cash. Core lending and trading were unaffected.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Incident was contained to the rewards subsystem.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Unexpected reward distribution transactions and operational key rotation cadence.

TypedRisks.name: Unaudited upgrade coverage gap
TypedRisks.description: Fluid has eight audits from four firms (PeckShield, StateMind, MixBytes, Cantina) but no formal verification, and no 2026-dated audit covering the 31 March 2026 module upgrade executed as proposal #126 at block 24779519. Upgrades shipping ahead of audit coverage is a recurring pattern.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Immunefi bug bounty under the Instadapp name paying up to $500,000 for smart contract critical and $100,000 for high.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Ratio of executed upgrade proposals to published audit reports covering them.

TypedRisks.name: Licensed deployment dependency via Jupiter Lend
TypedRisks.description: Jupiter Lend on Solana is a lending and borrowing protocol "powered by Fluid's modular Liquidity Layer", running up to 90% to 95% LTV with liquidation penalties as low as 0.1%. A failure of Fluid's engine propagates to a Solana venue Fluid does not itself operate, and reputational damage runs both ways. Exact licensing and revenue terms were not confirmed in sources fetched here.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Jupiter Lend markets are fully isolated with their own assets, risk parameters and curator, including a Bitwise x Ethena co-curated market.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Jupiter Lend market health and any Fluid engine incident that would apply to Solana deployments.

TypedRisks.name: DEX rebalancing turning impermanent loss permanent
TypedRisks.description: Fluid DEX automatically rebalances smart collateral and smart debt positions, which converts impermanent loss into realised permanent loss, an effect the team associates with LVR. DEX v2 is built to address this but launch has been held back pending market conditions.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Design works best on stablecoin and correlated pairs; DEX v2 pending, Solana DEX in final audit.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Realised loss versus fees earned on smart collateral and smart debt positions.

TypedRisks.name: Franchise contraction after consecutive incidents
TypedRisks.description: Lending TVL fell from $1.28b in February 2026 to $750.8m by 27 April 2026, a 41% decline, against a peak of $2.37b on 9 October 2025. Buybacks were paused after roughly 1.3% of supply was repurchased and FLUID emissions were cut.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Foundation forgoing $250,000 per month from March to June 2026; aWETH Redemption Protocol launched April 2026 with $10b initial capacity, processing over $440m of withdrawals.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Monthly lending TVL by chain, FLUID emissions schedule, and buyback resumption.

TypedRisks.name: Multi-chain expansion outpacing risk tooling
TypedRisks.description: Fluid runs on Ethereum, Arbitrum, Plasma, Base, Polygon and BNB Chain, and is extending to Solana, a Venus Flux deployment co-engineered on Fluid, and the Sui Hashi Bitcoin lending testnet. Each venue adds an oracle set, a bridge and a sequencer that the core team must monitor.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Per-chain isolated liquidity layers and per-vault parameters.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Number of live chains versus incident response times; per-chain TVL (Ethereum $527.7m, Arbitrum $131.2m, Plasma $107.6m, Base $32.4m, Polygon $4.7m as of 11 May 2026).

fluid.RiskPosture: Fluid is the most technically sophisticated protocol in this set and also the one with the most recent damage. Its shared Liquidity Layer and tick-based liquidation engine allow 80% to 95% LTVs with penalties as low as 0.1%, which is genuinely best in class, and Yearn's curation team scored it 1.4 out of 5.0, "Minimal Risk". The problem is not the engine, it is what gets plugged into it: Fluid repeatedly ends up holding almost the entire float of a third-party yield-bearing wrapper inside 6x loops, so an issuer failure at Resolv in March 2026 turned into $10m to $21m of Fluid bad debt and a 30% TVL fall in a day. Bad debt was made whole, but by discretionary loans and a team multisig drawing a credit line before the governance vote, which is a governance answer rather than a structural one, and the one-day timelock leaves lenders little room to act on such decisions. Today's book still shows top-five collateral at 69% and several markets above 90% utilization, so the same shape is in place, and the Jupiter Lend and Venus deployments extend that shape to venues Fluid does not run.

gearbox.name: Gearbox
gearbox.AssetStrategy:
Gearbox is the protocol where "supported asset" is least meaningful as a flat list. Liquidity providers deposit into an underlying-asset pool, for example a WETH, wstETH, USDC, USDT, DAI, GHO, crvUSD, WBTC, tBTC or DOLA pool, each pool owned by a named curator. A borrower opens a credit account, a smart contract wallet that holds borrowed funds plus their own collateral, and each pool is served by one or more credit managers that define, per credit manager, the exact list of tokens that may sit in the account and the liquidation threshold applied to each. On top of that, a credit account can only interact with the outside world through adapters, whitelisted contracts that translate a call into an allowed action against a specific integrated protocol such as Curve, Convex, Pendle, Balancer, Uniswap, Lido, Mellow or a specific ERC-4626 vault. The asset surface is therefore the cross product of collateral tokens with per-manager liquidation thresholds, quota limits set in the PoolQuotaKeeper which act as a per-collateral borrow cap, and the adapter whitelist. Gearbox documents its price layer as "Chainlink Price Feeds, Redstone Price Feeds as well as some composite smart contract oracles", and it documents that "the current version of Gearbox has isolated lending only, in which case the risk is contained within LP pools" ([Gearbox risks and T&C](https://docs.gearbox.finance/developers/risks-and-t-c-2), [Gearbox adapters and integrations](https://docs.gearbox.finance/core/adapters-integrations)). The interest rate model is a two-kink curve with an `isBorrowingMoreU2Forbidden` switch that hard-blocks borrowing past the second kink ([Gearbox interest rate model](https://docs.gearbox.finance/core/interest-rate-model)). All numeric values below were read live on 2026-07-26 from mainnet: 21 pools, 89 credit managers, 227 collateral tokens with liquidation thresholds, and 888 adapters, via the CreditAccountCompressor at 0x4115708Fc8fe6bB392De2e0C21c2C81dA2222394 and the pool and quota-keeper contracts. Gearbox TVL is roughly $18.4M ([DefiLlama Gearbox](https://defillama.com/protocol/gearbox)).

Column mapping for Gearbox: "Max LTV %" is not a Gearbox concept, so it is reported as n.a.; "Liq. threshold %" is the per-credit-manager liquidation threshold, reported as the observed range across credit managers where a token appears in more than one; "Borrow cap" is the PoolQuotaKeeper quota limit for that collateral in the named pool; there is no supply cap primitive.

TypedRisks.name: Curator sets unsafe risk parameters
TypedRisks.description: Curators act as Administrator over a Market Configurator and control every risk parameter including liquidation thresholds, quotas and the interest rate model. Wrong liquidation thresholds on allowed assets can make LP pools insolvent, and ChainSecurity notes the Configurator role is fully trusted and can configure most system parameters.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Administrator changes are subject to a 24-hour minimum timelock; curators must bear first loss via staking under the GIP-264 model; revenue split default 50% curator, 50% DAO.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Pending Market Configurator transactions in the 24-hour timelock, and curator stake size versus pool TVL.

TypedRisks.name: Emergency Admin bypasses the timelock
TypedRisks.description: The Emergency Admin role bypasses the 24-hour timelock and can pause a market, set debt limits to zero and forbid adapters or tokens. It cannot increase risk, but it can freeze a user's ability to manage a leveraged position at the worst moment.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Role is constrained to risk-reducing actions only; a whitelisted Emergency Liquidator can still liquidate when a market is paused.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Emergency Admin transactions and market pause events.

TypedRisks.name: Oracle failure causing cascading liquidations
TypedRisks.description: Gearbox's own risk page states a rogue oracle can cause cascading liquidations and bad debt, and the protocol relies on Chainlink, Redstone and composite smart contract oracles. Composite oracles that derive an exchange rate from another contract inherit that contract's failure modes.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Dual-oracle design pairs a Main Feed for liquidation with a Reserve Feed acting as a guardrail against incorrect or outdated valuations; Price Feed Store whitelisting is required to create a market.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Main Feed versus Reserve Feed deviation per asset, and feed staleness on Redstone push feeds.

TypedRisks.name: Liquidation cascade on LRT depeg
TypedRisks.description: Gearbox explicitly cites the April 2024 ezETH cascade as the motivating case for its Loss Policy, when rapid price falls outran liquidators. Leverage of up to 40x on a credit account means small collateral moves are enough to breach a health factor of 1.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Loss Policy blocks a liquidation that would create bad debt if the position is healthy under an aliased fundamental price; partial liquidation via a Deleverage Bot triggers at a configured minHF such as 1.05 with a reduced premium.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Count of accounts with health factor below 1.05, and frequency of Loss Policy blocked liquidations.

TypedRisks.name: Bad debt socialised onto LPs
TypedRisks.description: If a Credit Account is liquidated with Total Value below Total Debt, unclaimed protocol fees are burned first and any remaining loss is socialised by reducing the Diesel LP token exchange rate. Lenders, not borrowers, take the residual.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Fee buffer absorbs first; Loss Policy avoids realising losses at distressed prices; Gearbox reports no bad debt since inception in 2021.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Diesel token exchange rate; any non-monotonic move is a realised LP loss.

TypedRisks.name: Loss Policy pausing liquidations during a real repricing
TypedRisks.description: The aliased bad debt policy halts liquidation when a position is healthy at fundamental price even though it is underwater at market price. If the market price is correct and the peg never returns, the deferred loss is larger when it is finally realised.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Aliased pricing is configurable per market, so curators choose the fundamental reference; the fundamental check still permits liquidation when the asset is genuinely insolvent.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Duration and notional of positions sitting in Loss Policy blocked state, and market versus aliased price gap.

TypedRisks.name: Liquidator dependency and MEV
TypedRisks.description: Liquidations depend on third-party liquidators who Gearbox acknowledges may malfunction, and the risks page also flags sandwich and MEV extraction against protocol operations. In small accounts the liquidation premium may not cover gas, which historically left core contributors liquidating at their own expense.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Token-backed backstops, a Reserve Fund and the recruitment of more professional liquidators; partial liquidation is executed by a specialised Deleverage Bot.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Time from health factor below 1 to liquidation, and liquidator address diversity.

TypedRisks.name: Adapter and integration surface risk
TypedRisks.description: Credit Accounts reach into external protocols through adapters, and Gearbox says credit accounts can connect to assets that are not on DEXes or not even tokenised. Each adapter imports the security assumptions of the target protocol.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Strict adapter allowlists (kpk's handbook specifies allowlists plus utilisation caps and quota limits); Emergency Admin can forbid an adapter immediately; Bytecode Repository verification ensures only audited bytecode is deployed.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: New adapter deployments per market, and the number of distinct external protocols reachable from a single credit account.

TypedRisks.name: Concentration in a small set of curators
TypedRisks.description: Five curators including Invariant Group, Re7 and Maven11 manage over $1.5b, with Re7 alone running more than $700m to $800m across 100+ pools on 14 chains. Correlated curator behaviour or a single curator's operational failure affects a large share of the system.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Curators hold no custody and perform no active allocation, only parameter management; markets are isolated so a failure is contained within the affected pool.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Curator TVL share, and overlap of the same collateral assets across different curators' markets.

TypedRisks.name: Depeg of base or collateral assets
TypedRisks.description: Gearbox lists depeg of base assets as a named risk, and its curated markets accept synthetic dollars and tokenised treasuries such as Ethena sUSDe and USDe, Sky sUSDS, Midas mTBILL and mBASIS. Isolated lending contains the loss within the affected LP pool rather than the whole protocol.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Isolated pool architecture; per-asset quotas cap how much debt any one collateral can secure; Chaos Labs LT and LB methodology includes a circuit breaker for persistent deviations.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Secondary market price versus redemption value for each synthetic or tokenised asset.

TypedRisks.name: Lender exit blocked at full utilization
TypedRisks.description: Gearbox states plainly that an LP cannot withdraw if the pool is fully utilised. Under the Two-Kink interest rate model, curators can also set isBorrowingMoreU2Forbidden to cap borrowing past U2.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Utilization-dependent interest rate curve with a slope 3 penalty above U2 to force repayment; Tumbler rate keeper adjusts quota rates by epoch.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Pool utilization versus U1 and U2, and days spent above U2.

TypedRisks.name: Extreme chain sprawl
TypedRisks.description: Gearbox says it is deployed on 27 blockchains, "the most of any lending protocol", having added five chains and more than 25 markets under Permissionless. Every additional chain adds a sequencer, an oracle network and a liquidator set that must all work during a stress event.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Markets are isolated per chain and per curator; the team forks networks eight times a day to test against black swan events.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Per-chain TVL versus liquidator coverage, and chain-level incident history.

TypedRisks.name: Documentation and audit link integrity
TypedRisks.description: The security page lists audits by ChainSecurity, Consensys Diligence, Sigma Prime and ABDK but carries the note that "Links above are placeholders", so the published evidence trail is incomplete. Verifiable audit coverage is the main external check on a permissionless curator system.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Immunefi bug bounty paying up to $1,000,000 for critical; formal verification of critical math components; Bytecode Repository restricts deployment to audited bytecode.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Publication of resolved audit links and new audit reports for each V3.1 release.

TypedRisks.name: Regulatory and legal uncertainty
TypedRisks.description: Gearbox's own terms flag legal and regulatory uncertainty, and its curated markets increasingly hold tokenised treasury products such as mTBILL and mBASIS that sit closest to securities regulation. Curators are identifiable commercial entities rather than anonymous parties.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Isolated markets mean a regulated asset can be removed without touching other pools; Emergency Admin can forbid a token immediately.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Regulatory actions against tokenised treasury issuers or against curator entities.

TypedRisks.name: Governance transition and DAO abandonment of pools
TypedRisks.description: GIP-264 in August 2025 fully abandoned DAO-governed pools in favour of the Permissionless model, migrating to curators including kpk and Maven11. Users who chose Gearbox for DAO oversight now depend on commercial curator diligence instead.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Curators must bear first loss via staking; the DAO retains the Veto Admin rapid-response multisig and the 50% revenue share.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Share of TVL in DAO pools versus curator pools, and curator stake at risk.
