gearbox.RiskPosture: Gearbox has the strongest loss record of the four, with no bad debt since 2021 including through the April 2024 ezETH cascade where it was the single most affected venue with $33m liquidated and still turned a profit. Its protections are unusually concrete: a dual-oracle Main and Reserve feed, a Loss Policy that halts liquidation when a position is only underwater at a dislocated market price, partial liquidation via a Deleverage Bot at a reduced premium, per-asset quotas that cap how much debt any collateral can secure, formal verification of the math libraries and a $1,000,000 Immunefi bounty. The risk has instead moved to the counterparty layer. Since GIP-264, risk parameters are set by commercial curators such as K3 Capital, Re7 Labs, kpk and Chaos Labs, and Gearbox's own auditor notes the Configurator role is fully trusted; a 24-hour timelock is the only structural brake, and an Emergency Admin can bypass even that. Combine that with credit accounts reaching up to 40x across adapters into Mellow, Pendle, Ethena and Sky, and 27 chains to police, and the plausible failure mode is not a contract bug but one curator parameterising one exotic collateral badly.

stella.name: Stella
stella.AssetStrategy: Stella is the outlier in this set because it is largely dormant and its public disclosure effectively stops in 2024. Its model is a zero-borrowing-interest leveraged strategy protocol on Arbitrum: lenders deposit a single asset into either a Hyper or a Standard lend pool, and strategy users borrow that liquidity to run a leveraged position on a specific DEX or yield venue, paying the lender a share of profit rather than an interest rate. The unit of listing is therefore a strategy (a specific pool on a specific venue with a specific leverage cap) plus a small set of lendable underlying assets. Leverage limits are derived from a Collateral Factor and Borrow Factor per strategy rather than published per asset, and Stella states only that "the threshold variable is set to 0.97-0.98.5 based on each strategy" ([Stella leverage docs, page dated 2023-09-29](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/stella-yield/stella-strategy/leverage)). A distinctive and rarely seen mechanic is that every strategy position expires after 30 days from opening and becomes liquidatable at expiry regardless of health, in addition to becoming liquidatable when the Debt Ratio exceeds 100% ([Stella liquidation docs, page dated 2024-06-28](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/stella-yield/stella-strategy/liquidation)). Caps exist in two layers, since "each strategy operates with its own specific borrowing cap, in addition to the underlying asset's borrowing cap", but no numeric cap is published ([Stella lend docs](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/stella-yield/stella-lend/why-stella-lend-is-unique)). Staleness is material and should be stated plainly: the supported-strategies page is dated 2023-11-08, the supported-lend-assets page is dated 2023-09-26, the Stella data API at graph.stellaxyz.io returns HTTP error code 522 and is offline, and DefiLlama reports Stella TVL at roughly $443k, Arbitrum only ([Stella supported strategies](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/stella-yield/stella-strategy/supported-strategies), [Stella supported lend assets](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/stella-yield/stella-lend/supported-assets), [DefiLlama Stella](https://defillama.com/protocol/stella)).

TypedRisks.name: Unresolved Iron Bank debt overhang
TypedRisks.description: Alpha Homora owed Iron Bank $32.429m at the time of the 2021 exploit and still owed $31.947m as of 2 March 2023, of which only about 1.5% had been repaid. As of April 2024 user funds had been locked for over a year and their value exceeded $60m.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Repayment agreement of 20% of protocol fees, collateralised by 50m ALPHA; goodwill fund created for affected depositors; police cases filed.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Any repayment transactions to Iron Bank, and the status of the Keep3r multisig holding Iron Bank.

TypedRisks.name: Collateral value collapse against a fixed debt
TypedRisks.description: The 50m ALPHA pledged to Iron Bank was worth roughly $60m to $90m at the time of the agreement and had fallen to about $6m, a decline of more than 90%. Repayment ran at roughly $5,000 per month against a $32m obligation.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Alpha proposed alternative settlement terms and demanded return of 63,000,000 ALPHA in collateral.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: ALPHA price and the market value of the pledged collateral versus outstanding debt.

TypedRisks.name: Counterparty freezing user funds unilaterally
TypedRisks.description: On 1 March 2023 Iron Bank paused Alpha Homora's lending accounts, freezing roughly $41m of user funds on Ethereum, and stated it reserved the right to use those funds to offset the debt. This is a governance action by a third party over Stella's users' assets.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Depositors voted to stop negotiating, take goodwill funds and pursue legal action; a goodwill fund was set up.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Iron Bank market pause status and multisig ownership changes.

TypedRisks.name: Undercollateralized lending by design
TypedRisks.description: Stella deliberately enables undercollateralized loans by holding the LP token as collateral inside the contract. If that containment assumption breaks, lenders have no external claim on the borrower.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Collateral Factors are assigned per LP based on volatility and backtesting: 0.92 for Uniswap V3 and Trader Joe V2 pairs, 0.95 for Penpie LST PT positions.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Positions where Debt Ratio approaches the Collateral Factor limit, and any contract path allowing LP collateral to leave the vault.

TypedRisks.name: Discretionary leverage parameter setting
TypedRisks.description: Maximum leverage is derived from Collateral Factor and Borrow Factor which are "tailored by the Stella research team" on historical volatility, with a threshold variable normally set between 0.97 and 0.985 per strategy. This is a team judgement rather than an on-chain governed parameter.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Parameters are documented publicly per LP; extra collateral can be added by users to improve Debt Ratio.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Changes to published Collateral Factors and threshold values.

TypedRisks.name: Off-chain oracle dependency on centralised exchanges
TypedRisks.description: The Stella Trade price oracle is an off-chain mechanism that triggers the liquidation engine using a weighted median of centralised exchange prices, weighted Binance 3, Coinbase, Bybit and OKX 2 each, and Kucoin, Gate.io, MEXC and Kraken 1 each. An off-chain oracle is a trusted operator dependency, and exchange outages or wash trading feed straight into liquidation decisions.
TypedRisks.mitigation: A secondary on-chain oracle is described as a contingency in the event of primary oracle outage or failure.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Oracle uptime, deviation between the off-chain mark price and on-chain DEX prices, and exchange-specific outages.

TypedRisks.name: Liquidation on 30-day position expiry
TypedRisks.description: Positions are liquidated when the Debt Ratio exceeds its limit or when the loan expires after 30 days. Time-based forced closure is an unusual risk that can crystallise a loss for a user whose position was never unhealthy.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Expiry is disclosed in documentation and coverage of the protocol; users can add extra collateral or close early.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Count of positions approaching their 30-day expiry date.

TypedRisks.name: Lender withdrawal delay
TypedRisks.description: An intentional 2-day withdrawal delay applies on the lending side after each deposit, and adding assets during the delay restarts the countdown. Lenders cannot exit during a fast-moving stress event.
TypedRisks.mitigation: The delay is a deliberate anti-sandwich measure tied to daily yield distribution, disclosed in documentation.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Lending pool inflow timing versus stress events; ysToken transfer restrictions.

TypedRisks.name: Concentrated integration risk in a few Arbitrum venues
TypedRisks.description: Every listed strategy sits on Uniswap V3, Trader Joe V2, Camelot or Penpie, and Penpie positions carry the highest collateral factor at 0.95 despite Pendle PT maturity mechanics. A failure at any one venue affects a disproportionate share of a very small book.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Collateral factors differentiated by venue; strategies documented per LP.

maple.RiskPosture: Maple is the most credit heavy protocol in this set, and its risk is fundamentally about who is borrowing rather than about code. Maple's answer since then has been to move underwriting in house, require overcollateralisation, and lean on regulated custodians and a Reg D exemption to serve institutional and accredited money, which is a genuine improvement but shifts the exposure rather than removing it. What remains is a concentrated book, more than three quarters of collateral in BTC and XRP, a single externally owned Pool Delegate key, an impairment switch that can cut depositor value without a vote, and secondary liquidity too thin to absorb a large exit. Depositors should treat syrupUSDC as a credit fund with a token wrapper, not as a money market position.

TypedRisks.name: Contagion from an integrated external protocol
TypedRisks.description: Notional's leveraged vaults deposited user capital into third party pools, so a vulnerability outside Notional could destroy vault equity. This materialised on 3 November 2025 when the Balancer V2 hack wiped out five Notional vaults.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Post incident the affected vaults were closed and Notional V3 was wound down. Notional Exponent runs real time monitoring and exploit prevention with Hypernative.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Exploit alerts on any protocol a live vault deposits into, sudden change in vault share price

TypedRisks.name: Bad debt socialised onto lenders as a haircut
TypedRisks.description: When vault collateral is destroyed, the resulting bad debt is not absorbed by an insurance fund but passed to the lenders of the borrowed currency. In November 2025 ETH lenders took a 56.019% haircut on mainnet and 19.244% on Arbitrum.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Reserves are burned first, then the haircut is applied pro rata. Reserves proved far too small relative to the loss.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Reserve balance as a percentage of outstanding vault debt in each currency

TypedRisks.name: Reserve buffer far too small to absorb a tail loss
TypedRisks.description: Notional's protocol reserves were written to zero in the incident, roughly 100 thousand USD on mainnet and 18 thousand USD on Arbitrum, plus about 205 thousand USD and 161,450 USD of non ETH reserves converted to ETH. Against 632.8 ETH of mainnet bad debt and 80.2 ETH on Arbitrum, the buffer covered a small fraction of the loss.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Reserves fully applied before haircuts, remediation plan closing positions and migrating borrowers
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Ratio of reserve balances to total vault debt, growth rate of reserves versus growth of leveraged exposure

TypedRisks.name: Total loss of leveraged vault equity
TypedRisks.description: Leveraged vault holders sit in the first loss position and can be wiped out entirely. In the Balancer incident vault holders lost 100% of their positions.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Supply caps per vault, minimum borrow sizes, requirement that positions remain liquidatable, audits of each vault strategy
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Vault share price, vault utilisation against its cap

TypedRisks.name: Vault economic insolvency independent of exploit
TypedRisks.description: Notional documentation identifies economic risk where a vault strategy loses value faster than it can be liquidated, leaving the position insolvent. This is distinct from smart contract failure and arises from the strategy itself.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Supply caps, minimum borrow sizes, liquidatability requirement, per vault leverage limits
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Vault health factor distribution, time between liquidation trigger and execution

TypedRisks.name: Liquidation failure producing bad debt for nToken holders
TypedRisks.description: nToken holders are exposed to bad debt if the protocol fails to liquidate an undercollateralised account in time. The nToken absorbs the shortfall.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Collateral haircuts, debt buffers, liquidation incentives, oracle price deviation limits
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Number of accounts below the liquidation threshold that remain unliquidated, gas conditions during volatility

TypedRisks.name: nToken redemption risk under high utilisation
TypedRisks.description: nToken holders may be unable to redeem at fair value when lending market utilisation is high, because the underlying liquidity is committed to fCash. Exit then requires selling into a thin market or waiting.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Utilisation dependent interest rate curves, published redemption mechanics
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Lending market utilisation rate, nToken secondary market discount to NAV

TypedRisks.name: Interest rate risk on fCash positions
TypedRisks.description: fCash is a fixed rate claim whose present value moves inversely with market interest rates. A holder exiting before maturity can realise a loss even with no credit event.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Fixed maturities so the position pulls to par if held, oracle rate TWAPs used for valuation
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Change in implied fixed rates across maturities, mark to market on open fCash

TypedRisks.name: Oracle deviation and TWAP valuation risk
TypedRisks.description: Collateral valuation relies on external price oracles with deviation limits, and fCash valuation relies on oracle rate TWAPs. A manipulated or stale feed distorts both liquidation triggers and portfolio value.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Oracle price deviation limits, TWAP smoothing of fCash rates, supply caps
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Oracle deviation limit breaches, TWAP versus spot divergence

TypedRisks.name: Smart contract risk in core protocol and vault strategies
TypedRisks.description: Notional documentation identifies smart contract risk in both the core protocol and in the external protocols that vault strategies integrate with. The Balancer Vault Strategy was among the audited components and still produced total vault loss through the upstream protocol.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Multiple audits including Sherlock in October 2022 for leveraged vaults and the Balancer Vault Strategy, Immunefi bug bounty
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: New audit findings, unaudited vault deployments

TypedRisks.name: Governance parameter risk
TypedRisks.description: Collateral haircuts, debt buffers, supply caps and oracle deviation limits are all set by NOTE and sNOTE governance through NRCs and NIPs voted on Snapshot. Mis-set parameters directly determine how much bad debt a shock produces.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Formal proposal process, published parameter tables
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Parameter change proposals on Snapshot, gap between proposed and prevailing market volatility

TypedRisks.description: Notional V3 was wound down on both Ethereum mainnet and Arbitrum after the Balancer incident rather than recapitalised. Users had to exit and cross currency borrowers were migrated to Aave through individually deployed Gnosis Safes.

notional.RiskPosture: Notional's failure mode was composability, not its own code. Its lending and fCash machinery worked as designed, but its leveraged vaults had deposited user capital into Balancer V2, and when Balancer was exploited in November 2025 the loss travelled straight through: vault holders lost everything, the protocol's reserves proved to be a rounding error against the damage, and mainnet ETH lenders were haircut more than 56%. That is the important lesson, because it shows that in Notional's design the lenders, not an insurance fund, are the ultimate backstop. Rather than recapitalise, the team wound V3 down on both chains and migrated borrowers out to Aave. The successor, Notional Exponent, launched in January 2026 with Sherlock and MixBytes audits, a 250 thousand USD Immunefi bounty and Hypernative monitoring, but it is a new codebase with thin launch liquidity that again depends on external curators and strategy providers. Anyone underwriting Exponent is underwriting the same composability question with better monitoring and no track record yet.

pendle.name: Pendle Finance
pendle.AssetStrategy: Pendle is the volume leader in yield tokenization and its asset strategy is aggressive breadth: any yield-bearing asset that can be wrapped into a Standardized Yield (SY) token can be split into a Principal Token and a Yield Token with a fixed expiry, and Pendle lists across Ethereum, Arbitrum, BNB Chain, Base and Sonic. As of July 26, 2026, chain 1 alone has 58 active markets in the API. The composition of the current top book is telling: it is dominated not by liquid staking tokens but by newer synthetic dollar and RWA-flavoured assets (USDai, USDat, sUSDe, sUSDD, mAPOLLO, mHYPER, ynRWAx, superUSDC), with Lido wstETH the only large legacy LSD market and the only one running out to December 2027. The single largest market by liquidity is PT-USDai on Arbitrum at $50.4M, an order of magnitude above the next tier. What distinguishes Pendle from Spectra is the depth per market and the fact that its PT pricing has become infrastructure for other protocols: the Linear Discount Oracle is explicitly positioned as the recommended feed for money markets and has been adopted by Aave and Morpho curators including Gauntlet and Steakhouse ([Pendle oracle overview](https://docs.pendle.finance/pendle-v2-dev/Oracles/OracleOverview)).

TypedRisks.description: Chaos Labs found the linear discount oracle used to price Pendle PTs as collateral can systematically underprice or overprice them, with more than 1 billion USD of PT collateral relying on it, primarily in Spark Morpho Vaults. TypedRisks.name: Permissionless market registration abused by an integrator
TypedRisks.description: The Penpie exploit worked because the attacker permissionlessly registered a fake Pendle market and used it to inflate a staking balance in Penpie's reward harvesting function. Pendle's permissionless market creation was the enabling surface even though Pendle's own contracts were not broken.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Pendle paused all contracts on discovery, safeguarding roughly 105 million USD according to LlamaRisk, and Pendle stated its own funds were secure
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: New market registrations from unknown deployers, unusual staking balance growth in integrator contracts

TypedRisks.name: Single venue liquidity and ephemeral pools
TypedRisks.description: LlamaRisk notes that PT liquidity comes from a single source, the Pendle AMM, that pools are ephemeral because they expire at maturity, and that no centralised exchange supports PTs. Exiting a large PT position before maturity depends entirely on one venue.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Deep incentivised pools for major markets, ability to hold to maturity
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: PT pool depth and slippage on a representative clip size, days to maturity

TypedRisks.name: Negative yield and principal loss on YT and PT
TypedRisks.description: LlamaRisk states that negative yield and principal loss are possible outcomes for Pendle positions. YT decays to zero at maturity and PT can trade below its expected redemption value if the underlying loses value.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Fixed maturity structure, disclosure in Pendle documentation
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Realised underlying yield versus implied yield at purchase, YT time decay curve

TypedRisks.name: Bug bounty small relative to value at risk
TypedRisks.description: LlamaRisk observed that Pendle's Immunefi bug bounty maximum of 250 thousand USD sits against roughly 5 billion USD of TVL and stated the programme could benefit from being increased. A low maximum payout weakens the incentive for whitehats to disclose rather than exploit.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Audits by ChainSecurity in August 2024 (2 medium, 9 low) and Spearbit in July 2024 (1 high, 2 medium, 5 low), plus Ackee, Dedaub, Dingbats and Code4rena wardens
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Bug bounty maximum as a percentage of TVL, audit cadence against new contract deployments

TypedRisks.name: Securities classification of Principal Tokens
TypedRisks.description: LlamaRisk records that Pendle's operating entity is domiciled in the British Virgin Islands and that the protocol relies on a 2023 opinion from a Singapore law firm that PTs are not securities. That is a single jurisdiction opinion supporting an instrument that is economically a zero coupon bond.
TypedRisks.mitigation: BVI domicile, external legal opinion, no securities enforcement action documented in the source
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: New regulatory guidance on tokenised fixed income, changes in the venues willing to list PTs

TypedRisks.name: Severe TVL contraction from the cycle peak
TypedRisks.description: Pendle TVL stood at about 935.95 million USD, against a peak of about 6.5 billion USD in June 2024 recorded by LlamaRisk. Falling TVL thins PT pool liquidity and raises exit slippage precisely when holders most want to leave.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Multi chain deployment spreading liquidity across Ethereum, Arbitrum, Plasma and others
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Total TVL trend, TVL per chain, PT pool depth per market

TypedRisks.name: Conflict of interest in third party risk assessment
TypedRisks.description: Chaos Labs disclosed in its Aave governance post that Pendle compensated Chaos Labs for the referenced risk reports. The risk parameters that gate more than 1 billion USD of PT collateral were recommended by a party paid by the issuer.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Public disclosure of the relationship in the governance thread, parallel independent review by LlamaRisk

pendle.RiskPosture: Pendle's own core contracts have never been drained, and PendleMarketV3 is immutable apart from pausing, which is a real strength. The risk lives everywhere else. Governance is concentrated in a 2 of 4 multisig and a single guardian key with no timelock, which was useful in September 2024 when Pendle paused everything within a day of the Penpie exploit and protected around 105 million USD, but the same power could be turned the other way. The bigger systemic issue is that PTs became collateral across Spark, Morpho, Aave and others, priced by a discount oracle that Chaos Labs showed can drift far enough for borrowers to walk away with debt, on markets running liquidation LTVs above 91%. Add underlying concentration in sUSDe and USD0++, issuers who can change redemption terms overnight, liquidity that exists only on Pendle's own AMM, and TVL that has fallen to under 1 billion USD from a 6.5 billion USD peak, and the profile is a technically sound protocol carrying other people's risks. Treat Pendle exposure as exposure to the specific underlying and to the lending market accepting the PT, not to Pendle in the abstract.

TypedRisks.name: Protocol sunset and abandonment of core development
TypedRisks.description: On 26 October 2023 the Sense team announced it would sunset the protocol after 18 months and cease core contributions, citing that the DeFi market lacked consistent demand for fixed rates. The UI was open sourced for community use.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Advance notice, open sourcing of the interface, published withdrawal instructions

TypedRisks.name: Loss of hosted interface after 1 December 2023
TypedRisks.description: Users were directed to withdraw through app.sense.finance by 1 December 2023, after which Sense relinquished hosting of the interface. Any remaining position must be recovered by interacting with contracts directly.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Open sourced UI that anyone can self host, contracts remain onchain and noncustodial
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Availability of the hosted app, existence of a community maintained frontend

TypedRisks.name: Unmaintained contracts with live admin powers
TypedRisks.description: Admin privileges over the protocol include adjusting guarded launch caps, toggling permissionless mode, verifying adapters, onboarding adapter factories, backfilling Scale, pausing the Divider and pausing adapters, and updating the Periphery. These powers sit with a 2 of 3 multisig on Ethereum mainnet that no longer has an active core team behind it.
TypedRisks.mitigation: 2 of 3 multisig at 0xDd76360C26Eaf63AFCF3a8d2c0121F13AE864D57, guarded launch restricting the Divider to Verified Adapters
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Any transaction from the admin multisig, changes to the multisig signer set

TypedRisks.name: Backfill Scale admin power over yield accounting
TypedRisks.description: The admin can Backfill Scale, the abstract metric the Divider uses to decide how Target is split between PT and YT holders. Whoever holds that power can effectively set the payout split of a series.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Multisig control rather than a single key, documented as an explicit admin privilege
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Backfill Scale transactions, unexpected changes in redemption values at settlement

TypedRisks.name: Adapter verification is a trusted centralised gate
TypedRisks.description: Sense distinguishes Verified Adapters, checked by the Sense team, from Unverified Adapters which the documentation says are unverified or deemed unsafe and could be controlled by malicious actors. With the team gone, no new verification happens.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Guarded launch means the Divider interfaces only with Verified Adapters until permissionless mode is enabled
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Whether Divider.addAdapter permissionless mode has been enabled, adapters onboarded after October 2023

TypedRisks.name: Adapter discretion over the scale value
TypedRisks.description: Sense documentation states the adapter has full discretion in how and when it determines the scale value, and the Divider queries the adapter for scales on collects and redemptions. A faulty or hostile adapter can therefore misallocate Target between PT and YT holders.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Adapter verification, required overrides of scale, getUnderlyingPrice, wrapUnderlying and unwrapTarget on BaseAdapter
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Scale values reported by each adapter versus the observable Target to Underlying exchange rate

TypedRisks.name: Third party conversion risk between Target and Underlying
TypedRisks.description: Sense only holds the Target asset, so all users are exposed to the risk that the Target cannot be converted back into the Underlying. Sense gives the example that Compound cDAI or Aave aDAI may not be convertible to DAI when a user wants to exit.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Position can be held in Target terms rather than exiting to underlying, documented and disclosed
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Utilisation and liquidity of the underlying lending market, any withdrawal freeze at Compound or Aave

TypedRisks.name: Balancer V2 dependency through the Space AMM

sense.RiskPosture: Sense is a discontinued protocol, and that is the dominant fact about its risk profile. It never suffered a documented exploit, it was audited eight times by credible firms including Spearbit and Sherlock, and it was noncustodial throughout, so the technical foundation was sound. What killed it was demand: the team concluded in October 2023 that DeFi simply did not want fixed rates consistently enough to sustain the product, wound it down, and open sourced the interface. Anyone still holding a Sense position is now dealing with unmaintained contracts, a hosted frontend that was switched off on 1 December 2023, and a 2 of 3 multisig that retains real powers including pausing the Divider and backfilling the Scale value that determines how much Target each PT and YT holder receives. Layered on top are the dependencies Sense always had, on Balancer V2 for the Space AMM and on Compound or Aave for converting Target back to Underlying. The residual risk is not that Sense will be hacked, it is that no one is left to respond if something goes wrong.

spectra.name: Spectra
spectra.AssetStrategy: Spectra is the permissionless end of the yield tokenization spectrum. Any ERC-4626 interest-bearing token can be wrapped into a PT and YT pair with no listing gate, and the protocol runs on nine networks: Ethereum mainnet, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, BNB Chain, Avalanche, HyperEVM, Katana and Sonic, per the pool API endpoints that returned data at `https://app.spectra.finance/api/v1/{network}/pools`. Liquidity sits in Curve StableSwap-NG and twocrypto-NG pools, with a `RateAdjustmentOracle` feeding the expected PT price into the AMM so the bonding curve only has to price the deviation of the realized implied rate from the expected rate ([Spectra rate adjusted StableSwap docs](https://dev.spectra.finance/technical-reference/spectras-automated-market-makers/rate-adjusted-stableswap-pools)). The trade-off versus Pendle is stark on scale: the entire Spectra pool set returned 25 pools, and the largest, PT-yvvbUSDC on Katana, holds $380,545.80 TVL, roughly 1/130th of Pendle's largest market. The asset mix skews toward long-tail and new-chain assets (Katana vault bridge USDC and USDT, Jarvis synthetic euro, YieldNest RWA baskets, Avant avUSD on Avalanche) rather than blue chip LSDs. Spectra also formalizes negative-yield handling through a `ptRate` variable that writes down the PT's par value if the underlying IBT ever registers negative interest ([Spectra rate adjusted StableSwap docs](https://dev.spectra.finance/technical-reference/spectras-automated-market-makers/rate-adjusted-stableswap-pools)).

TypedRisks.name: Peripheral router contract compromise
TypedRisks.description: On 23 July 2024 an attacker exploited a command in Spectra's routing utility contract that let users enter and exit pools with a token of their choice, sweeping funds once a user approved a transaction. The core protocol contracts were unaffected.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Router contracts were terminated, the app was disabled and Principal Token contracts paused, an incident response plan is in place
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Unusual approvals to Spectra router addresses, any new router deployment without audit

TypedRisks.name: Social engineering directing users into malicious approvals
TypedRisks.description: The July 2024 attack was amplified by a Discord user making false claims about problems with Spectra's YT contracts, prompting users to withdraw and therefore approve the malicious transaction. The attack surface was human as much as technical.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Incident response plan, direct communication channels, coordination with exchanges and security teams
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Impersonation or panic messaging in official community channels, spikes in approval transactions after such messaging

TypedRisks.name: Pause authority over Principal Token contracts
TypedRisks.description: During the July 2024 incident Spectra paused Principal Token contracts to prevent token exchanges at the Curve pool level, then unpaused them roughly six hours later. That confirms a privileged party can halt PT transfers at will.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Pause was used defensively and reversed the same day, response documented publicly
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Pause events on PT contracts, duration of any pause

TypedRisks.name: Permissionless pool creation with no vetting
TypedRisks.description: Anyone can open a Spectra pool with any ERC-4626 interest bearing token, specifying only a maturity date and target APR, with no voting or human gated process. There is no screening of the yield source behind a listed market.

TypedRisks.description: Spectra documents negative yield risk: the share value of an ERC-4626 interest bearing token can fall, which reduces the assets backing the Principal Token. A PT is not principal protected if the vault behind it loses value.

rows: At approximately 3:00 PM UTC on Ethereum mainnet an attacker exploited a command in Spectra's router utility contract that allowed users to enter and exit pools with a token of their choice, sweeping funds after users approved the transaction. A Discord user made false claims about YT contract problems to prompt withdrawals. Four wallets were impacted and core protocol contracts were unaffected.

Spectra disabled the app, terminated the router contracts, paused Principal Token contracts to block exchanges at the Curve pool level, then unpaused at about 9 PM UTC and reinstated the app on 24 July. Authorities, exchanges and security teams were contacted, and Spectra sent the attacker an onchain offer to close the case if 90% of funds were returned. Attacker address 0x53635bf7b92b9512f6de0eb7450b26d5d1ad9a4c.

Resolv, a major source of ERC-4626 collateral tokenised on Spectra, was exploited. A compromised SERVICE_ROLE private key held in AWS KMS combined with a completeSwap function that performed no onchain check on the ratio between deposited funds and minted tokens allowed 80 million USR to be minted from roughly 300 thousand USDC, a 266 to 1 ratio.

USR fell below 0.025 USD at its lowest point. The attacker extracted about 11,400 ETH worth roughly 24 million USD and still held about 36 million USR worth an estimated 2 million USD. Downstream damage was amplified by a donation attack on Morpho vaults using a hardcoded 1 USD oracle for USR and wstUSR. Spectra is not named among the affected protocols in the OAK Research analysis, so direct Spectra losses are n.a.

spectra.RiskPosture:
Spectra is a small, permissionless protocol whose core contracts have held up well and whose risk sits almost entirely at the edges. Three independent audit engagements, Code4rena, Pashov and Sherlock, produced no high severity findings, and the one exploit it suffered in July 2024 hit a peripheral router contract and four wallets rather than the protocol itself, costing around 168 ETH and being contained within six hours. The structural exposures are different in kind. Anyone can list any ERC-4626 token as a market with no vetting, and Spectra's own documentation says it has no control over what users contribute, so the protocol's real credit quality is whatever its underlyings happen to be. That became concrete on 22 March 2026 when Resolv, a major source of Spectra collateral, was exploited for 80 million USR of unbacked mint and saw USR trade below three cents. On top of that, TVL has fallen to about 28 million USD spread thinly across twelve chains, with more than 85% sitting on Hemi and Flare rather than Ethereum. Spectra should be judged one market at a time, because the protocol offers no protection at all against a bad underlying.

notes.Implementation notes for M6 and M7:
## Build the asset table as the join surface, not a list

Every risk row in this dataset already carries `link_assets_matched`. That means the M6 asset row and the M7 risk drill down are the same object viewed twice. Build one `AssetRiskRow` model that holds the parameters and the attached risks together, and render it in both tabs. If M6 and M7 end up with two separate data shapes, the bidirectional link in M7 item 6 becomes a fuzzy string match at runtime, which is exactly the failure this dataset was compiled to avoid.

## Do not overstuff the asset tab

The 12 column asset table in this file is the full data model, not the default view. Show 6 columns by default (Asset, Role, Max LTV, Liq. threshold, Oracle, composite risk bar) and put the rest behind the row drill down. Cap the visible list at 8 rows with a show all toggle. The current failure is a flat 15 row undifferentiated stack; replacing it with a flat 20 row stack that has more columns is not progress. The segmented control from `components/agent/trade/TradeModeSelector.tsx` is the right shell.

## Sentinel values that will look like bugs

Several protocols use `1` as a borrow cap to mean borrowing is disabled. Aave does this on weETH, rsETH, osETH, rETH, tBTC, LBTC and XAUt; Radiant does it on every borrowable reserve as part of the wind down. Render these as `Borrowing disabled`, never as a cap of one token. Similarly, `LTV 0` with a live liquidation threshold means LTV was withdrawn while existing positions are grandfathered. That is a risk signal worth a badge, not an empty cell. Aave carries it on USDe, sUSDe, DAI, LINK, XAUt and osETH.

## Four entities are not in a steady state

* Radiant Capital began a DAO wind down on 1 June 2026, and borrowing is disabled protocol wide. No published LTV or threshold values exist; the table uses stored on chain values, labelled as stored, not live. Show a wind down banner on the entity, not just on individual rows.
* Notional Finance V3 is winding down. The 3 November 2025 Balancer V2 hack impaired five leveraged vaults, produced 632.8 ETH of bad debt on mainnet and 80.2 ETH on Arbitrum, and haircut ETH lenders 56.019 percent on mainnet and 19.244 percent on Arbitrum. The forward product is Notional Exponent, live 26 January 2026 with two USDC vaults. This is a data correctness problem for M0 and M1, not just M6. Whatever the seed currently says about Notional is describing a product that is being retired.
* Sense Finance sunset in October 2023 with a 1 December 2023 withdrawal deadline. Every asset row is deprecated. It is the one Credit entity that correctly hides its Asset coverage tab today; keep that behaviour and show a sunset card instead.
* Stella is effectively dormant: no per asset collateral factor, borrow factor, cap or liquidation discount has ever been published, the docs date from 2023 and 2024, the strategies API returns 522, and TVL is about 443k USD. Report it as dormant rather than rendering an empty parameter grid.

## Severity matrix, M7 item 4

Every risk carries a likelihood and an impact on a three point scale, so the matrix is a 3x3 grid with dots, not a scatter plot needing synthetic coordinates. `risk_profile.likelihood_impact_matrix` gives the per cell counts, so cell sizing can be computed without walking the full risk list. Cluster collision in the high/high cell is the main layout problem: Aave, Morpho, Radiant, Stella, Notional and Pendle each carry four critical risks. Jitter within the cell or use a count badge that expands.

## Scorecard methodology must be visible

M7 item 3 requires the methodology to be visible on hover or click, never an unexplained number. The honest version is the weighted counts in the risk category distribution table above: severity weights of 4, 3, 2, 1 summed per category. Do not normalise these into a 0 to 100 score without showing the inputs, and do not compare composites across tags: a Fixed Income protocol and a Leveraged Yield protocol carry structurally different risk shapes, so a single ranked league table would be misleading.

## Incident history rail, M7 item 7

52 documented incidents across the 14 entities, all with dates, amounts where published, and outcomes. The heaviest are Radiant (January 2024 flash loan and the October 2024 multisig compromise at about 50m USD), Aave (the April 2026 Kelp rsETH exploit with 123m to 230m USD of bad debt), Compound (seven incidents going back to the November 2020 DAI oracle liquidations), and Maple (the 2022 Orthogonal Trading default at about 36m USD written off, against the Auros episode which was repaid in full on 8 November 2023). Show both outcomes: a default that was repaid and a default that was written off are very different credit facts and the rail is the only place that distinction becomes visible.

## Cross-tag risk is the finding worth surfacing

The shared risk drivers table above is the most interesting output of this research. Chainlink touches six entities, Lido six, Sky four, Pendle five and Morpho four, across all three tags. The current UI shows risk as a per entity property, which hides the fact that a single oracle or issuer failure moves a third of the Credit sector at once. If M6 and M7 ship only per entity views, this insight is lost. Consider a sector level risk driver panel, or at minimum a badge on each risk row showing how many other Credit entities share the same driver. The generic `<RelationshipExplorer>` built in M9 can render this with no new component work, which is a good argument for building M9's shell before finalising M7.
